Clinical Vignette: Raymond

Raymond is a 53-year-old married man who has driven city buses for nearly two decades. He knows his routes the way most people know their own handwriting - automatically, without thought. Passengers have always been a comfort to him, a kind of moving community he shepherds through the city each day. That ease, that quiet pride in his work, is something he is only now beginning to understand he has lost.

Fourteen months ago, Raymond was sexually assaulted. He had stayed late after a union meeting held in a community center, and a man he recognized vaguely from the neighborhood followed him into the parking garage and raped him at knifepoint. Raymond did not fight back. He has not forgiven himself for this. He drove home afterward, sat in his truck in the driveway for two hours, and said nothing to his wife when he finally came inside. He told no one for three weeks. When he did speak - to a crisis line, in the middle of the night, while his wife slept - he hung up before the counselor finished her first sentence.

Raymond eventually told his wife, Denise, in fragments, over the course of several painful conversations. She responded with love and steadiness, but Raymond finds her tenderness almost unbearable. Physical closeness between them has become rare. He does not explain this to her in any way that satisfies either of them. He simply moves away, quietly, and she has learned not to reach for him.

At work, Raymond functions - barely. He sits behind the wheel for eight hours and moves through the city on autopilot, which is both a mercy and a source of dread. Certain intersections are dangerous for him: the street near the community center, the parking garage entrance visible from the Route 14 loop. When he passes these, his hands tighten on the wheel and his vision narrows. Twice in the past six months he has had to pull over, open the door, and breathe through what he describes as "the feeling that I'm back there." He does not call these panic attacks. He calls them "episodes," and he is ashamed of each one.

He sleeps poorly. When he does sleep, he often wakes at two or three in the morning with his heart hammering, the details of the assault vivid and immediate, the smell of the garage present in the room. He gets up, sits in the kitchen, and watches television with the volume low until dawn. He has done this so often that the kitchen chair has become his side of the bed in some private, unspoken way.

Raymond has stopped attending the union meetings he once looked forward to. He has withdrawn from the small circle of friends he and Denise socialized with on weekends. He drinks more than he used to - not dramatically, he would say, but a few beers every night instead of the occasional one. He does not think of it as a problem. He thinks of it as the only thing that quiets the noise in his head by ten o'clock.

What troubles Raymond most, and what he articulates with a kind of raw precision, is the belief that he is no longer himself. He describes the man he was before the assault as someone competent, steady, good at his job, good to his wife. He does not recognize that man anymore. He feels contaminated in a way he cannot fully put into words, only that he does not want to be touched, does not want to be seen, and is quietly convinced that if Denise truly understood what happened - not just the facts, but what it meant - she would see him the way he sees himself. He has never asked her whether this is true. He is afraid she would try to reassure him, and he would not believe her, and then there would be nothing left to hold onto.
